l: Agamemnon, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Fragment #67—Scholiast on Euripides, Orestes 249: Steischorus says that
s: Agamemnon was regarded as a son of Pleisthenes and Cleolla in one Hesiodic genealogy. As Tyndareus’s son-in-law, he wooed Helen for his brother Menelaus.

l: Aegisthus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Fragment #67—Scholiast on Euripides, Orestes 249: Steischorus says that
s: Aegisthus became Clytaemnestra’s lover after she deserted Agamemnon.

l: Helen, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Fragment #67—Scholiast on Euripides, Orestes 249: Steischorus says that
s: Helen is described as an Argive maid with the beauty of Aphrodite and the sparkling eyes of the Graces. Many heroes sought her in marriage, and Menelaus won her after Tyndareus required the suitors to swear an oath; she later bore Hermione and Nicostratus to Menelaus.

l: Menelaus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Fragment #67—Scholiast on Euripides, Orestes 249: Steischorus says that
s: Menelaus, son of Atreus, prevailed over the other suitors for Helen because he offered the greatest gifts and was greatest among the Achaeans in possessions. He married Helen and became the father of Hermione and Nicostratus.

l: Castor, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Fragment #67—Scholiast on Euripides, Orestes 249: Steischorus says that
s: Castor, called horse-taming, was a son of Tyndareus and brother of Polydeuces. He and Polydeuces would have made Philoctetes their brother by force, and Menelaus sent messages to them during his suit for Helen.

l: Polydeuces, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Fragment #67—Scholiast on Euripides, Orestes 249: Steischorus says that
s: Polydeuces, called prize-winning, was a son of Tyndareus and brother of Castor. He and Castor would have made Philoctetes their brother by force, and Menelaus communicated with them while seeking Helen.

l: Zeus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Fragment #67—Scholiast on Euripides, Orestes 249: Steischorus says that
s: Zeus planned to mingle storm and tempest over the earth and destroy the race of mortal men, including the demigods, so that gods and mortals would no longer mate. He also laid toil and sorrow upon those born of immortals and mortals, directed the destructive storm, and struck Eetion with a thunderbolt.

l: suitors of Helen, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Fragment #67—Scholiast on Euripides, Orestes 249: Steischorus says that
s: The suitors of Helen came from many places, including Ithaca, Phylace, Athens, Salamis, Euboea, Crete, and elsewhere, bringing gifts or promising possessions and tribute. Tyndareus required them to swear that they would defend the marriage against anyone who took Helen by force, and Menelaus ultimately defeated them all in the suit.

l: Odysseus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Fragment #67—Scholiast on Euripides, Orestes 249: Steischorus says that
s: Odysseus, son of Laertes, sought Helen in marriage from Ithaca. He sent no gifts because he believed that Menelaus would win through his greater wealth and his continuing messages to Castor and Polydeuces.

l: Achilles, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Fragment #67—Scholiast on Euripides, Orestes 249: Steischorus says that
s: Achilles was still a boy while Chiron tended him on wooded Pelion. Hesiod’s account says that no man, including Menelaus, would have prevailed in the suit for Helen if Achilles had found her unmarried.

l: demigods, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Fragment #67—Scholiast on Euripides, Orestes 249: Steischorus says that
s: The demigods were the children of gods and mortal women or men. Zeus planned to destroy their race and imposed toil and sorrow upon those born from immortals and mortals.

l: gods, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Fragment #67—Scholiast on Euripides, Orestes 249: Steischorus says that
s: The gods were divided through strife while Zeus contemplated the destruction of the demigods. They were to live apart from mortals, as they had done before, rather than continue mating with them.

l: Zeus’s plan to destroy the demigods, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Fragment #67—Scholiast on Euripides, Orestes 249: Steischorus says that
s: Zeus’s plan was to mingle storm and tempest over the earth, bring mortal life to an end, and destroy the children of gods and mortals. He intended thereby to prevent gods from mating with mortals and to restore their separation.

l: Poseidon, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Fragment #67—Scholiast on Euripides, Orestes 249: Steischorus says that
s: Poseidon is presented as the father of Butes and as the father of Minyas. He also helped Apollo raise the wall of the well-built city.

l: Heracles, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Fragment #67—Scholiast on Euripides, Orestes 249: Steischorus says that
s: Heracles is called the great-hearted offspring of Alcaeus and is the only figure named as daring to fight a formidable warrior with the spear. He loved Deianeira, who bore him Hyllus, Glenus, Ctesippus, and Odites, and he encountered Auge while seeking Laomedon’s horses and fighting the Amazons.

l: Meleager, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Fragment #67—Scholiast on Euripides, Orestes 249: Steischorus says that
s: Meleager, son of Oeneus and Althaea and loved by Ares, was a powerful hero whose eyes shone with portentous fire. He slew the Calydonian boar but was later killed by Apollo while fighting the Curetes for Calydon.

l: Calydonian boar, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Fragment #67—Scholiast on Euripides, Orestes 249: Steischorus says that
s: The Calydonian boar was a fierce, destructive beast with gleaming tusks. Meleager slew it in high Calydon.

l: Apollo, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Fragment #67—Scholiast on Euripides, Orestes 249: Steischorus says that
s: Apollo killed Meleager with his hands and arrows while Meleager was fighting the Curetes for Calydon. Apollo also killed Hyacinthus unintentionally with a ruthless discus and, in another account, loved Ileus.

l: Helen’s suitor oath, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Fragment #67—Scholiast on Euripides, Orestes 249: Steischorus says that
s: Helen’s suitor oath required all the suitors to swear, with unmixed libations, that none would act independently concerning Helen’s marriage. If anyone took her by force, all the others were to follow and punish him.

l: marriage of Helen and Menelaus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Fragment #67—Scholiast on Euripides, Orestes 249: Steischorus says that
s: The marriage of Helen and Menelaus followed Menelaus’s victory over the other suitors in the contest for her hand. Menelaus prevailed because he offered the greatest gifts, and Helen later bore him Hermione and Nicostratus.

l: Calydonian boar hunt, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Fragment #67—Scholiast on Euripides, Orestes 249: Steischorus says that
s: The Calydonian boar hunt is represented through Meleager’s killing of the fierce boar at Calydon. Meleager was later slain by Apollo while fighting the Curetes over Calydon.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE SHIELD OF HERACLES
s: Alcmena bears twin sons, Heracles by Zeus and Iphiclus by Amphitryon, after Zeus and Amphitryon separately share her bed in one night. Heracles and Iolaus prepare for battle against Cycnus and Ares, while Athena instructs Heracles to kill Cycnus and wound Ares without taking their horses or armor. Hephaestus’s elaborate Shield of Heracles depicts war, divine figures, death, cities, agriculture, contests, and Ocean surrounding the rim. Heracles and Cycnus finally meet in battle, but the unit ends before the fight’s outcome is given.

l: Alcmena, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE SHIELD OF HERACLES
s: Alcmena, the daughter of Electryon, leaves her home and comes to Thebes with Amphitryon. She is praised for her beauty, height, wisdom, and devotion to Amphitryon, and she bears twin sons: Heracles by Zeus and Iphiclus by Amphitryon.

l: Amphitryon, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE SHIELD OF HERACLES
s: Amphitryon comes to Thebes as a suppliant after violently killing Electryon over oxen and is required to avenge the deaths of Alcmena’s brothers. After completing the task of burning the villages of the Taphians and Teleboans, he returns to Alcmena and fathers Iphiclus.

l: Zeus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE SHIELD OF HERACLES
s: Zeus plans to beget a defender of gods and mortals and shares Alcmena’s bed during the same night that Amphitryon does. Through Zeus’s union with Alcmena, Heracles is born, and Zeus later gives Heracles power to slay Cycnus.

l: Heracles, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE SHIELD OF HERACLES
s: Heracles is the stronger and more formidable son of Alcmena, born from her union with Zeus. He arms himself with divine equipment, including a breastplate from Athena and a shield made by Hephaestus, then goes with Iolaus to fight Cycnus and Ares.

l: Iolaus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE SHIELD OF HERACLES
s: Iolaus accompanies Heracles as his charioteer and fellow warrior. He takes the reins, drives the chariot, and prepares to help Heracles confront Cycnus and Ares.

l: Cycnus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE SHIELD OF HERACLES
s: Cycnus, the son of Ares, confronts Heracles and Iolaus near the grove of Apollo, intending to kill them and strip their armor. He refuses Heracles’ warning to yield, leaps from his chariot, and begins the battle against Heracles.

l: Ares, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE SHIELD OF HERACLES
s: Ares appears with Cycnus, armed and eager for war, and urges his footmen into battle. Athena tells Heracles to watch Ares closely and wound him when he is exposed below his shield, but not to take his horses or armor.

l: Athena, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE SHIELD OF HERACLES
s: Athena comes to Heracles and Iolaus as they prepare for battle and encourages them. She tells Heracles that Zeus grants him power to kill Cycnus, instructs him how to wound Ares, and then joins them in the chariot with victory and renown.

l: Hephaestus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE SHIELD OF HERACLES
s: Hephaestus makes Heracles’ bronze greaves and fashions the adamantine helmet and the great shield. His work on the shield includes intricate images of warfare, gods, death, cities, agriculture, contests, and Ocean.

l: Thebes, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE SHIELD OF HERACLES
s: Thebes is the seven-gated city where Amphitryon and Alcmena live and where their twin sons are born. Its walls are associated with the protection of the Earth-Shaker, and it is also represented among the shield’s imagery through a city with seven golden gates.

l: Shield of Heracles, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE SHIELD OF HERACLES
s: The Shield of Heracles is a vast, glittering shield made with enamel, ivory, electrum, gold, cyanus, and adamant. It depicts Fear, Strife, battle, monsters, animals, gods, Perseus, doomed warriors, festive cities, farming, contests, and Ocean with swans and fish around the rim.

l: shield-making by Hephaestus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE SHIELD OF HERACLES
s: Hephaestus makes and fits the shield at Zeus’s command. The shield’s workmanship includes precious materials and detailed figures that appear almost alive, including fighting warriors, moving animals, Perseus in flight, and scenes of human work and celebration.

l: war against Cycnus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE SHIELD OF HERACLES
s: Heracles and Iolaus drive toward Cycnus and Ares after Athena gives Heracles instructions for the encounter. Cycnus refuses to withdraw, and the opposing warriors leap from their chariots and begin fighting as Zeus thunders and sends drops of blood as a battle sign.

l: Heracles and Iolaus’s victory over Cycnus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE SHIELD OF HERACLES
s: The unit establishes that Zeus gives Heracles power to slay Cycnus and that Iolaus helps him as charioteer and warrior. Their battle with Cycnus begins, but no victory or death is reported before the unit ends.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 402-412) As two lions 1806 on either side of a slain deer spring
s: Heracles kills Cycnus by striking him in the unguarded neck with a spear. Ares attacks Heracles in grief for Cycnus, but Athene diverts Ares’ spear and Heracles wounds Ares in the thigh. Ares is carried away to Olympus, while Heracles and Iolaus strip Cycnus’ armour and go to Trachis. Ceyx buries Cycnus, but Anaurus later washes away the grave and memorial at Apollo’s command.

l: Heracles, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 402-412) As two lions 1806 on either side of a slain deer spring
s: Heracles strikes Cycnus in the neck beneath the chin and kills him. He then faces Ares and wounds him in the exposed thigh before going with Iolaus to Trachis.

l: Cycnus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 402-412) As two lions 1806 on either side of a slain deer spring
s: Cycnus attacks Heracles with a brazen spear, but it does not break Heracles’ shield. Heracles kills him with a spear-thrust to the neck, and Cycnus’ armour is later stripped from his body.

l: Ares, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 402-412) As two lions 1806 on either side of a slain deer spring
s: Ares attacks Heracles in grief over Cycnus’ death, but Athene turns aside his spear. Heracles wounds Ares deeply in the thigh, after which Panic and Dread carry him by chariot to Olympus.

l: Athena, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 402-412) As two lions 1806 on either side of a slain deer spring
s: Athene warns Ares to stop fighting Heracles, but he does not obey. She diverts the force of his spear and later goes to Olympus and her father’s house.

l: Cycnus’ burial, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 402-412) As two lions 1806 on either side of a slain deer spring
s: Ceyx buries Cycnus, and many people gather to honour Ceyx. Anaurus, swollen by a rain-storm, later destroys Cycnus’ grave and memorial because Apollo commanded it.

l: Heracles and Iolaus’s victory over Cycnus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 402-412) As two lions 1806 on either side of a slain deer spring
s: Heracles and Cycnus rush at one another like lions or vultures fighting over prey. Cycnus’ spear fails against Heracles’ shield, and Heracles kills him with a powerful spear-thrust to the unguarded neck.

l: the battle between Heracles and Ares, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 402-412) As two lions 1806 on either side of a slain deer spring
s: Ares and Heracles charge at one another after Cycnus falls. Athene intervenes on Heracles’ behalf, and Heracles wounds Ares in the thigh, causing Ares to be carried away to Olympus.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE MARRIAGE OF CEYX
s: The Marriage of Ceyx is attributed to Hesiod, though some grammar-school boys disputed its authorship. It concerns Heracles, who landed from the Argo to seek water and was left behind in Magnesia near Aphetae. Heracles is also shown as a regular visitor to Ceyx’s house at Trachis. The poem mentions horse-driving Ceyx, calls tables tripods, and describes wood being brought from the forest to be burned after a feast.

l: Hesiod, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE MARRIAGE OF CEYX
s: Hesiod is said to have written The Marriage of Ceyx and to have included accounts of Heracles, Ceyx, tripods used as tables, and wood brought for burning. One source notes that grammar-school boys disputed the poem’s attribution to him.

l: Marriage of Ceyx, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE MARRIAGE OF CEYX
s: The Marriage of Ceyx describes Heracles landing from the Argo to look for water and being left behind in Magnesia near Aphetae. It also presents Heracles visiting Ceyx’s house at Trachis, refers to horse-driving Ceyx, calls tables tripods, and describes wood being brought from the forest to be burned.

l: Ceyx, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE MARRIAGE OF CEYX
s: Ceyx is associated with Trachis and is visited there by Heracles. He is described as horse-driving, and his house is represented as a place where feasts are held.

l: Heracles, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE MARRIAGE OF CEYX
s: Heracles landed from the Argo to look for water and was left behind in Magnesia near Aphetae because of his desertion there. He is also represented as repeatedly visiting Ceyx’s house at Trachis and speaking about the good attending the feasts of the good.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE GREAT EOIAE
s: The fragments of the Great Eoiae preserve genealogies, heroic episodes, and accounts of divine and human figures. They concern figures including Heracles, Telamon, Endymion, Melampus, Phineus, and the descendants of Phrixus. Hesiod is cited as the poet of the Great Eoiae, which includes stories about Heracles and about Hermes and Battus. In the story of Hermes and Battus, Hermes steals cattle, tests Battus’s secrecy, and changes him into a rock when he reveals the theft.

l: The Great Eoiae, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE GREAT EOIAE
s: The Great Eoiae is cited for genealogies and stories involving Argos, Epidaurus, Heracles, Telamon, Polycaon, Endymion, Melampus, Phineus, and the children of Phrixus. It tells how Hermes stole cattle and changed Battus into a rock after Battus revealed where the cattle were hidden.

l: Hesiod, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE GREAT EOIAE
s: Hesiod is said to have composed or related material in the Great Eoiae. He is cited for portraying Heracles as both the most toilful and the most excellent, for saying that Phineus was blinded after telling Phrixus the way, and for the story of Hermes and Battus.

l: Heracles, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE GREAT EOIAE
s: Heracles is described as the son of Zeus and Alcmene, and as destined to be the most toilful and the most excellent. He is also identified as the father of Hyllus and is said to have been entertained by Telamon while wearing his lion-skin and praying.

l: Hermes, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE GREAT EOIAE
s: Hermes stole twelve heifers, a hundred unyoked cows, and a bull from the herds associated with Apollo and Admetus. He tested Battus by disguising himself and asking whether Battus had seen stolen cattle; after Battus revealed the theft, Hermes struck him with his staff and changed him into a rock.

l: Battus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE GREAT EOIAE
s: Battus lived on a rock and recognized the stolen cattle being driven past. Hermes promised him a reward for secrecy, but Battus later accepted a robe and disclosed that he had seen the cattle, after which Hermes changed him into a rock.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE MELAMPODIA
s: The Melampodia concerns the seers Calchas, Mopsus, and Teiresias, as well as the fate of Amphilochus. Calchas challenges Mopsus to count the figs on a wild fig-tree, but dies after Mopsus gives the correct answer. Teiresias is said to have lived through seven generations, changed sex after killing snakes, and judged the relative pleasure of men and women in intercourse. Hera blinds Teiresias for his answer, while Zeus grants him prophetic power.

l: The Melampodia, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE MELAMPODIA
s: The Melampodia includes accounts of Calchas's contest with Mopsus, Teiresias's long life and prophetic experiences, and the deaths of Calchas and Amphilochus. It also contains passages concerning feasting, omens, Mares, Mantes, Iphiclus, Phylacus, and Chalcis.

l: Calchas, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE MELAMPODIA
s: Calchas returned from Troy with Amphilochus and came on foot to the place near Clarus. After finding Mopsus to be a greater seer, he asked him to determine the number of figs on a small wild fig-tree; when Mopsus answered correctly, Calchas died of vexation.

l: Mopsus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE MELAMPODIA
s: Mopsus, the son of Manto and grandson of Teiresias, was a seer greater than Calchas. He correctly stated that the wild fig-tree bore ten thousand figs, filling a bushel with one fig left over.

l: Teiresias, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE MELAMPODIA
s: Teiresias is said to have lived through seven generations, from the time of Cadmus to the time of Eteocles and Polyneices, though others say nine. After killing a female snake and then a male snake, he changed from a man to a woman and back again. He judged that a man enjoys one part of sexual pleasure while a woman enjoys all ten parts, and he was blinded by Hera but given prophetic power by Zeus.

l: Zeus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE MELAMPODIA
s: Zeus selected Teiresias, together with Hera, to decide whether men or women receive greater pleasure in intercourse. After Hera blinded Teiresias for his answer, Zeus granted him the power of prophecy.

l: Hera, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE MELAMPODIA
s: Hera selected Teiresias, together with Zeus, to judge whether men or women receive greater pleasure in intercourse. She became angry at his answer and blinded him.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, AEGIMIUS
s: The fragments of the “Aegimius” concern Phrixus’s reception by Aeetes, Thetis’s testing of her children by Peleus, and the story of Io, Zeus, Hera, Argus, and Hermes. They also attribute accounts of Io and her transformation, the killing of Argus, and oaths concerning love to Hesiod or the author of the “Aegimius.” Another fragment describes a speaker’s place of refreshment, and the final fragment explains the name “Three-fold People” for the Pelasgi, Achaeans, and Dorians who settled in Crete.

l: Aegimius, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, AEGIMIUS
s: The author of the “Aegimius” says that Phrixus was received without intermediary because of the fleece and that, after the sacrifice, he purified the fleece before entering Aeetes’s halls. The second book says that Thetis threw her children by Peleus into a cauldron to discover where they were mortal. The work is also associated with an account of a speaker’s place of refreshment and with the settlement of three Hellenic tribes in Crete.

l: Thetis, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, AEGIMIUS
s: Thetis threw the children she had by Peleus into a cauldron of water because she wished to learn where they were mortal. After many had perished, Peleus prevented her from throwing Achilles into the cauldron.

l: Peleus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, AEGIMIUS
s: Peleus became annoyed after many of the children he had by Thetis perished. He prevented Thetis from throwing Achilles into the cauldron.

l: Achilles, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, AEGIMIUS
s: Achilles was one of the children of Thetis and Peleus. Peleus prevented Thetis from throwing him into the cauldron.

l: Io, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, AEGIMIUS
s: Io was said by Hesiod and Acusilaus to be the daughter of Peiren and a priestess of Hera. Zeus seduced her, and Hera discovered this; Zeus touched Io and changed her into a white cow. Hera set Argus to watch her.

l: Hera, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, AEGIMIUS
s: Hera employed Io as a priestess and discovered that Zeus had seduced her. After Zeus changed Io into a white cow, Hera set the strong watcher Argus over her.

l: Zeus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, AEGIMIUS
s: Zeus seduced Io and, after being discovered by Hera, touched her and changed her into a white cow while swearing that he had not had intercourse with her. He was also said to have called Abantis Euboea after the cow.

l: Argus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, AEGIMIUS
s: Argus was a great and strong watcher set over Io by Hera. He had four eyes, looked in every direction, and never slept while keeping watch. Hermes slew him according to Hesiod’s tale.

l: Hermes, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, AEGIMIUS
s: Hermes slew Argus, the herdsman of Io, according to Hesiod’s tale.

l: Hesiod, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, AEGIMIUS
s: Hesiod and Acusilaus are said to have identified Io as the daughter of Peiren. Hesiod also said that oaths concerning the secret deeds of the Cyprian were without penalty for men, and his tale says that Hermes slew Argus. The “Aegimius” is described as being by Hesiod or Cercops of Miletus.

l: Crete, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, AEGIMIUS
s: Three Hellenic tribes, the Pelasgi, Achaeans, and Dorians, were said to have settled in Crete. They were called the Three-fold People because they divided the land into three parts.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, FRAGMENTS OF UNKNOWN POSITION
s: The unit preserves 23 fragments quoted by ancient authors and commentators. Linus is described as the lovely son of Urania, mourned and invoked by singers and harpers at feasts and dances. Other fragments concern Apollo, gods, Muses, mythic peoples, customs, conduct, and proverbial sayings. Hesiod is called a servant of the sweet Muses, and it is said that those whom the immortals honor also receive good report from mortals.

l: Linus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, FRAGMENTS OF UNKNOWN POSITION
s: Linus is described as the very lovely son of Urania. Singers and harpers bewail him at feasts and dances, invoking him at both their beginnings and their endings.

l: Hesiod, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, FRAGMENTS OF UNKNOWN POSITION
s: Hesiod is called the servant of the sweet Muses. It is said that whoever the immortals honor is also followed by the good report of mortals.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, DOUBTFUL FRAGMENTS
s: This unit presents ten doubtful fragments attributed or reported by Galen, a Homeric scholiast, a Pindaric scholiast, Julian, Servius, Plato, Clement of Alexandria, Apollonius, Stephanus of Byzantium, and another Pindaric scholiast. The fragments concern Zeus taking sense from Athamas, the grinding of yellow grain, and a song addressed to Phoebus Apollo by Delos singers identified as the speaker and Homer. They also mention starvation, the Hesperides and their golden apples, gifts moving gods and princes, the sun’s bright light on the seventh day, water mixed with Ocean’s streams, the sons of Orchomenus, and Telemon’s slaying of Melanippe.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE HOMERIC HYMNS / I. TO DIONYSUS 2501
s: The hymn addresses Dionysus and recounts conflicting claims about where he was born. It says that Zeus secretly gave birth to him far from humans, at a high, wooded Nysa near the streams of Aegyptus. Zeus ordains that mortals will sacrifice perfect hecatombs to Dionysus at his feasts every three years. The singers ask Dionysus to be favorable and say that no one who remembers him may call holy song to mind.

l: Dionysus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE HOMERIC HYMNS / I. TO DIONYSUS 2501
s: Dionysus is said to have been born in several different places, though these claims are declared false. He is called Heaven-born, Insewn, and Inspirer of frenzied women, and mortals are ordained to sacrifice perfect hecatombs to him at his feasts every three years.

l: Zeus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE HOMERIC HYMNS / I. TO DIONYSUS 2501
s: Zeus, the thunder-lover and Father of men and gods, secretly gave birth to Dionysus far from men. He spoke, nodded with his dark brows, and ordained that mortals would sacrifice to Dionysus at his feasts.

l: Semele, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE HOMERIC HYMNS / I. TO DIONYSUS 2501
s: Semele is said by some to have borne Dionysus to Zeus. She is called Dionysus's mother and is also called Thyone.

l: Nysa, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE HOMERIC HYMNS / I. TO DIONYSUS 2501
s: Nysa is described as a very high mountain richly grown with woods. It is said to be far off in Phoenice, near the streams of Aegyptus, and is the place associated with Dionysus's true birth.

l: Dionysus's birth, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE HOMERIC HYMNS / I. TO DIONYSUS 2501
s: Different accounts place Dionysus's birth at Dracanum, windy Icarus, Naxos, the river Alpheus, and Thebes, but the hymn says these accounts are false. It states that Zeus gave birth to Dionysus secretly and far from men, at Nysa.

l: holy song, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE HOMERIC HYMNS / I. TO DIONYSUS 2501
s: The singers invoke Dionysus as they begin and end a strain. They say that no one who forgets him may call holy song to mind.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, II. TO DEMETER
s: Demeter’s daughter Persephone is abducted by Hades with Zeus’s permission, and Demeter searches for her while mourning. Hecate and Helios reveal the abduction to Demeter, who withdraws from the gods and disguises herself as Doso in Eleusis. There she nurses Demophoon and attempts to make him immortal, but Metaneira discovers the act and interrupts it. Demeter then reveals herself, commands the people of Eleusis to build her temple and altar, and promises to teach her rites.

l: Demeter, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, II. TO DEMETER
s: Demeter loses Persephone when Hades abducts her, and she searches the earth for her daughter while refusing ambrosia, nectar, food, and drink. She disguises herself as Doso, enters the household of Celeus, nurses Demophoon, and becomes enraged when Metaneira interrupts her attempt to make him immortal. She reveals her divine identity and commands the people to build her a temple and altar, promising to teach her rites.

l: Persephone, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, II. TO DEMETER
s: Persephone gathers flowers with the daughters of Oceanus when the earth opens and Hades carries her away in his golden chariot. She cries out for her father, and her abduction causes Demeter profound grief.

l: Hades, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, II. TO DEMETER
s: Hades, called Aidoneus and the Host of Many, abducts Persephone with Zeus’s permission and carries her unwillingly to his realm in his chariot. Helios describes him as Persephone’s appointed husband and lord of the dead.

l: Zeus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, II. TO DEMETER
s: Zeus gives Persephone to Hades and permits Hades to carry her away. He is described as the cloud-gathering, loud-thunderer Son of Cronos, and Demeter becomes angry with him for the abduction.

l: Hecate, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, II. TO DEMETER
s: Hecate hears Persephone’s cries from her cave when the other gods and mortals do not. On the tenth day, she meets Demeter, reports what she heard, and accompanies her to Helios.

l: Helios, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, II. TO DEMETER
s: Helios, the bright son of Hyperion and watcher of gods and mortals, hears Persephone’s cries and sees what happened. He tells Demeter that Zeus gave Persephone to Hades and that Hades carried her away.

l: Eleusis, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, II. TO DEMETER
s: Eleusis is the place ruled by Celeus where Demeter arrives in disguise. Its women draw water from the Maiden Well, and Demeter later commands its people to build her temple and altar.

l: Celeus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, II. TO DEMETER
s: Celeus is the wise ruler of fragrant Eleusis and the father of Callidice, Cleisidice, Demo, and Callithoe. His household receives Demeter in disguise, and he later calls the people together to carry out her command to build a temple and altar.

l: Metaneira, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, II. TO DEMETER
s: Metaneira is Celeus’s wife and the mother of the late-born Demophoon. She welcomes Doso into her household to nurse him, but watches at night and sees Demeter placing him in the fire, causing Demeter to abandon her attempt to make him immortal.

l: Iambe, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, II. TO DEMETER
s: Iambe gives the disguised Demeter a jointed seat covered with a silvery fleece. Through quips and jokes, she makes the grieving goddess smile, laugh, and regain some cheer.

l: Demophoon, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, II. TO DEMETER
s: Demophoon is the late-born son of Metaneira and Celeus, whom Demeter nurses in their palace. He grows like an immortal being while Demeter tends him, but he remains mortal after Metaneira interrupts the goddess’s work.

l: the golden chariot, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, II. TO DEMETER
s: Hades uses his golden chariot and immortal horses to seize Persephone and carry her to his realm. After Helios speaks to Demeter, he calls his own horses and drives his chariot away.

l: kykeon draught, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, II. TO DEMETER
s: The kykeon draught is prepared for Demeter from meal, water, and soft mint after she refuses red wine. Demeter drinks it in order to observe the sacrament.

l: Demeter’s temple, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, II. TO DEMETER
s: Demeter commands the people of Eleusis to build her a great temple below the city and its sheer wall, on a rising hillock above Callichorus. Celeus summons the people, who obey and construct it.

l: Demeter’s altar, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, II. TO DEMETER
s: Demeter commands that an altar be built beneath her temple on the rising hillock above Callichorus. Celeus orders the people to build it, and they carry out his command.

l: the Eleusinian Mysteries, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, II. TO DEMETER
s: Demeter promises to teach her rites to the people of Eleusis. She says that performing them reverently will win the favour of her heart.

l: abduction of Persephone, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, II. TO DEMETER
s: Persephone is taken by Hades when the earth opens beneath her as she gathers flowers. Zeus has given her to Hades, and Hades carries her away unwillingly while she cries for her father.

l: Demeter’s search for Persephone, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, II. TO DEMETER
s: Demeter searches for Persephone across the earth and sea for nine days, carrying flaming torches and asking gods and mortals for news. On the tenth day, Hecate directs her to Helios, who tells her what happened.

l: Demeter’s mourning, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, II. TO DEMETER
s: Demeter grieves intensely after Persephone’s abduction, tears at her hair, casts off her cloak, and refuses ambrosia, nectar, food, and drink. Her grief and anger lead her to avoid the gods and withdraw among mortals.

l: Demeter’s disguise as Doso, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, II. TO DEMETER
s: Demeter disguises herself as an old mortal woman named Doso and claims to have escaped pirates from Crete. In this form, she seeks work and enters Celeus’s household.

l: Demeter’s nursing of Demophoon, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, II. TO DEMETER
s: As Doso, Demeter takes Demophoon into her care and nurses him. She feeds him ambrosia by day, breathes sweetly upon him, and tends him at night in the fire.

l: attempt to make Demophoon immortal, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, II. TO DEMETER
s: Demeter attempts to make Demophoon deathless and ageless by placing him in the fire at night. Metaneira sees her and cries out, so Demeter removes the child and declares that he can no longer escape death, though he will retain lasting honour.

l: building of Demeter’s temple, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, II. TO DEMETER
s: After revealing herself, Demeter orders the people to build her a great temple and an altar at Eleusis. Celeus gathers the people, and they promptly obey his command.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 301-320) Now when they had finished building and had drawn back
s: Demeter causes a devastating famine by hiding the seed because Persephone has been taken from her, threatening both mankind and the honors of the gods. Zeus sends Hermes to bring Persephone from Hades, but Persephone has eaten a pomegranate seed and must spend one-third of each year below the earth and two-thirds with Demeter and the gods. Demeter restores the earth’s fertility and teaches the Eleusinian Mysteries to Triptolemus, Diocles, Eumolpus, and Celeus. The unit presents the seasonal return of Persephone and the establishment of rites at Eleusis.

l: Demeter, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 301-320) Now when they had finished building and had drawn back
s: Demeter withdraws from the gods and causes famine by keeping the seed hidden, refusing to let fruit spring from the earth until she sees Persephone. After Persephone returns, Demeter restores fertility to the land and teaches her rites and mysteries to human kings.

l: Persephone, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 301-320) Now when they had finished building and had drawn back
s: Persephone is brought from Hades to rejoin Demeter, but she has eaten a pomegranate seed and therefore must spend one-third of each year in darkness and gloom and two-thirds with her mother and the other deathless gods. She recounts that Hades carried her away beneath the earth while she was gathering flowers.

l: Zeus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 301-320) Now when they had finished building and had drawn back
s: Zeus recognizes that Demeter’s famine threatens mankind and the honors of the gods. He sends Iris, the gods, and finally Hermes to persuade or arrange for Persephone’s return, and he establishes the division of Persephone’s time between the underworld and the upper world.

l: Hades, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 301-320) Now when they had finished building and had drawn back
s: Hades, ruler over the departed and brother of Zeus, obeys Zeus’s command to release Persephone. He secretly gives her a sweet pomegranate seed and tells her that she will rule among the deathless gods and receive great honors.

l: Hermes, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 301-320) Now when they had finished building and had drawn back
s: Hermes travels to Erebus at Zeus’s command and uses soft words to persuade Hades to release Persephone. He drives the immortal horses and brings Persephone back to Demeter’s temple.

l: the gods of Olympus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 301-320) Now when they had finished building and had drawn back
s: The deathless gods repeatedly visit Demeter, offering beautiful gifts and whatever rights she might choose, but they cannot persuade her to end her anger. They later receive Demeter and Persephone again among them, while Persephone remains absent for one-third of the year.

l: men, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 301-320) Now when they had finished building and had drawn back
s: Mankind suffers from the famine caused by Demeter, as the earth produces no crops. Zeus fears that the human race will be destroyed and that people will no longer provide gifts and sacrifices to the gods.

l: Eleusis, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 301-320) Now when they had finished building and had drawn back
s: Eleusis contains Demeter’s fragrant temple and rocky stronghold, where she dwells apart from the gods during her anger. It is also associated with the rites and mysteries that Demeter teaches after restoring the earth’s fertility.

l: Erebus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 301-320) Now when they had finished building and had drawn back
s: Erebus is the dark region from which Hermes is commanded to bring Persephone back to the gods. Persephone is described as returning from Erebus to the light after Hermes reaches Hades’s house.

l: the underworld, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 301-320) Now when they had finished building and had drawn back
s: The underworld is the hidden realm beneath the earth where Hades rules and Persephone is taken. Persephone must return there for one-third of every year after eating the pomegranate seed.

l: earth, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 301-320) Now when they had finished building and had drawn back
s: The earth becomes barren when Demeter hides the seed, leaving fields without sprouting grain and the plain of Rharus leafless. After Demeter agrees to return, the earth produces leaves, flowers, and abundant grain.

l: the pomegranate seed, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 301-320) Now when they had finished building and had drawn back
s: Hades secretly gives Persephone a sweet pomegranate seed, which she eats before leaving the underworld. Because she has tasted it, she cannot remain permanently with Demeter and must return below for part of each year.

l: the famine, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 301-320) Now when they had finished building and had drawn back
s: The famine is caused by Demeter’s grief and anger over Persephone’s absence. It threatens to destroy mankind and to end the gifts and sacrifices owed to the gods, but it ends when Persephone’s return is arranged.

l: abduction of Persephone, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 301-320) Now when they had finished building and had drawn back
s: Persephone says that while she and other maidens were gathering flowers, the earth opened and Hades sprang forth in his golden chariot to carry her away beneath the earth. She describes the abduction as having been carried out through the deep plan of Zeus.

l: Persephone’s seasonal return, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 301-320) Now when they had finished building and had drawn back
s: Persephone returns to Demeter after Hermes brings her from the underworld. Because she has eaten the pomegranate seed, she spends two parts of the year with Demeter and the deathless gods and one part in darkness and gloom.

l: the Eleusinian Mysteries, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 301-320) Now when they had finished building and had drawn back
s: Demeter teaches the Eleusinian Mysteries and the conduct of her rites to Triptolemus, Diocles, Eumolpus, Celeus, and others. The mysteries are described as sacred and not to be transgressed, investigated, or spoken of; those who have seen them are called blessed, while the uninitiated lack comparable good after death.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, III. TO DELIAN APOLLO
s: The hymn celebrates Apollo’s birth on Delos, where Leto gives birth after traveling through many lands and securing the island’s promise to receive him. Apollo grows immediately into a powerful god who declares his love for the lyre and bow and his role in revealing Zeus’s will. Delos becomes honored through Apollo’s temple, sacrifices, and the gatherings of the Ionians, whose songs and dances praise the gods. The poet-narrator asks the maidens of Delos to identify the blind singer of Chios as the sweetest singer and promises to spread their renown.

l: Apollo, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, III. TO DELIAN APOLLO
s: Apollo is the far-shooting son of Zeus and Leto, born on Delos after Leto’s long labor. The gods honor and fear him, and he declares that the lyre and curved bow will always be dear to him while he proclaims the unfailing will of Zeus.

l: Leto, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, III. TO DELIAN APOLLO
s: Leto alone remains beside Apollo when he enters Zeus’s house, where she unstrings his bow and removes his quiver. During her labor she travels among many lands before securing Delos as Apollo’s birthplace, and she gives birth while holding a palm tree on the island.

l: Delos, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, III. TO DELIAN APOLLO
s: Delos agrees to receive Apollo after Leto promises that he will establish there a fragrant altar, precinct, and oracle. Although the island is rocky and poor, it becomes greatly honored, laden with gold at Apollo’s birth, and the gathering place of the Ionians.

l: Artemis, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, III. TO DELIAN APOLLO
s: Artemis is the daughter of Leto and Zeus and the sister of Apollo. She is associated with arrows and is praised alongside Apollo and Leto by the girls of Delos.

l: Zeus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, III. TO DELIAN APOLLO
s: Zeus is Apollo’s father and receives him in his house, where he gives him nectar in a golden cup. Apollo declares that he will reveal Zeus’s unfailing will to men.

l: the Ionians, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, III. TO DELIAN APOLLO
s: The long-robed Ionians gather on Delos with their children and wives to honor Apollo. They delight him with boxing, dancing, and song, and their gathering appears so splendid that a person might think them deathless and ageless.

l: Chios, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, III. TO DELIAN APOLLO
s: Chios is identified as the home of a blind man whose songs are declared supreme. The poet-narrator instructs the maidens of Delos to name this blind singer as the sweetest singer who comes there.

l: Cynthus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, III. TO DELIAN APOLLO
s: Cynthus is the rocky hill on Delos beside which Leto rests against a palm tree when she gives birth to Apollo. Apollo later walks upon craggy Cynthus.

l: Apollo’s temple, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, III. TO DELIAN APOLLO
s: Apollo’s temple on Delos is promised to bring the island honor, crowds, hecatombs, and the continual savor of rich sacrifice. The hymn also says that Apollo has many temples and wooded groves in other places.

l: Apollo’s lyre, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, III. TO DELIAN APOLLO
s: Apollo declares that the lyre will always be dear to him, together with the curved bow. The lyre therefore forms part of his announced divine identity and musical power.

l: birth of Apollo, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, III. TO DELIAN APOLLO
s: Apollo’s birth takes place on Delos after Leto swears that he will establish an altar, precinct, and oracle there. The goddesses wash and swathe him, Themis gives him nectar and ambrosia, and he immediately becomes too powerful to be held by cords or bands.

l: Leto’s labor, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, III. TO DELIAN APOLLO
s: Leto suffers nine days and nine nights of extraordinary labor while Hera prevents Eilithyia from hearing of her trouble. Iris brings Eilithyia to Delos, after which the pains seize Leto and she gives birth.

l: Apollo’s arrival at Delos, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, III. TO DELIAN APOLLO
s: Apollo’s arrival at Delos follows Leto’s search for a willing land and the island’s acceptance of her promise. At his birth Delos rejoices, becomes covered with gold, and is chosen by Apollo as his dwelling above the other islands and shores.

l: Delian festival, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, III. TO DELIAN APOLLO
s: The Delian gathering brings the long-robed Ionians, their children, and their wives together in Apollo’s honor. Boxing, dancing, song, and the performances of the girls of Delos form part of this celebrated assembly.

l: song and praise, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, III. TO DELIAN APOLLO
s: Song and praise are devoted to Apollo, Leto, and Artemis, and the girls of Delos sing about men and women of former times. Their songs imitate every human tongue so closely that each listener might think he himself were singing.

l: Apollo’s oracle, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, III. TO DELIAN APOLLO
s: Delos asks Leto to swear that Apollo will first build there a glorious temple to serve as an oracle for men. Leto swears that Apollo will have his altar and precinct on the island, which he will honor above all.

l: old man and divine singer (in Colophon), Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, III. TO DELIAN APOLLO
s: The blind singer dwells in rocky Chios and is praised as having supreme lays. The maidens of Delos are instructed to identify him, in one voice, as the sweetest singer who comes to their gathering.

l: the poet-narrator, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, III. TO DELIAN APOLLO
s: The poet-narrator praises Apollo, Leto, Delos, and the Delian maidens throughout the hymn. He asks the maidens to remember him and promises to carry their renown throughout the earth wherever he travels.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, TO PYTHIAN APOLLO—
s: Apollo searches through Greece for a place to establish an oracle and chooses Crisa beneath Parnassus after Telphusa deceives him about her spring. He builds a temple there, slays the dragoness that threatens men, and establishes Pytho as the site of his sanctuary and prophetic authority. Apollo then captures a ship of Cretans in the form of a dolphin and brings them to Crisa to serve as ministers of his temple. He instructs them to receive sacrifices, preserve righteousness, and proclaim the will of the gods.

l: Apollo, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, TO PYTHIAN APOLLO—
s: Apollo travels through many regions seeking a place for an oracle, establishes his temple at Crisa, and kills the dragoness near its spring. He brings the Cretans to serve his sanctuary, gives them instructions, and promises to provide them with abundant offerings.

l: Zeus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, TO PYTHIAN APOLLO—
s: Zeus is Apollo’s father and the cloud-gathering ruler whose will sends a strong west wind to carry the Cretan ship toward Crisa. Hera also compares the strength of her desired child with Zeus’s strength.

l: Hera, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, TO PYTHIAN APOLLO—
s: Hera becomes angry when Zeus gives birth to Athena without her and decides to bear a child without Zeus. She prays to Earth, Heaven, and the Titan gods, and later gives the newborn Typhaon to the dragoness.

l: Typhoeus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, TO PYTHIAN APOLLO—
s: Typhaon is born to Hera without Zeus and is described as a cruel plague to men. Hera gives him to the dragoness, who raises him as another source of harm.

l: the dragoness, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, TO PYTHIAN APOLLO—
s: The dragoness raises Typhaon and causes great harm to men and their sheep. Apollo shoots and kills her near the spring, after which her body rots in the sunlight and the place is called Pytho.

l: the Cretans, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, TO PYTHIAN APOLLO—
s: The Cretans, sailing from Cnossos for trade, are carried against their will to Crisa by Apollo. They obey his commands, establish an altar, follow him while singing the Ie Paean, and become ministers of his temple.

l: Telphusa, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, TO PYTHIAN APOLLO—
s: Telphusa persuades Apollo to build his temple at Crisa rather than beside her spring because she wants to retain renown for herself. When Apollo discovers her deception, he covers her streams with rocks and establishes an altar nearby.

l: Pytho, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, TO PYTHIAN APOLLO—
s: Pytho is the place beneath Parnassus where Apollo establishes his sanctuary after killing the dragoness. Its name is explained by the power of the sun that caused the monster to rot there, and Apollo is called Pythian.

l: Crisa, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, TO PYTHIAN APOLLO—
s: Crisa is the western-facing place beneath snowy Parnassus where Apollo decides to build his temple and oracle. The Cretan ship reaches its harbor, and the Cretans settle there as ministers of Apollo.

l: Parnassus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, TO PYTHIAN APOLLO—
s: Parnassus is the mountain beneath whose glades Apollo establishes his temple at Crisa. The Cretans follow Apollo to its ridge and reach the sanctuary where they are to dwell.

l: the temple of Apollo, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, TO PYTHIAN APOLLO—
s: Apollo’s temple at Crisa is founded as an oracle where people from Peloponnesus, Europe, and the islands will bring perfect hecatombs and seek unfailing counsel. Trophonius and Agamedes lay its stone footing, and countless people build the temple.

l: Apollo’s oracle, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, TO PYTHIAN APOLLO—
s: Apollo’s oracle is established at Crisa to answer people who come from many lands seeking divine counsel. Apollo promises to deliver counsel that cannot fail from his rich temple.

l: the Cretan ship, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, TO PYTHIAN APOLLO—
s: Apollo boards the Cretan ship in the shape of a dolphin and makes it tremble while the crew sails helplessly. He guides it past the coasts of Peloponnesus to Crisa, where it grounds on the shore.

l: Apollo’s journey in search of an oracle site, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, TO PYTHIAN APOLLO—
s: Apollo travels from Pieria through many places, including Iolcus, Euboea, Thebe, Onchestus, Cephissus, Ocalea, Haliartus, and Telphusa, seeking a suitable site for an oracle. He finally selects Crisa beneath Parnassus.

l: the founding of the temple at Crisa, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, TO PYTHIAN APOLLO—
s: Apollo lays out the foundations of his temple at Crisa, and Trophonius and Agamedes set its stone footing. Human communities then build the temple of wrought stones so that it will be celebrated forever.

l: Apollo’s slaying of the dragoness, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, TO PYTHIAN APOLLO—
s: Apollo kills the dragoness near the sweet-flowing spring with an arrow from his strong bow. He declares that she will no longer plague men and sheep, and her death gives the place the name Pytho.

l: Apollo’s capture of the Cretans, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, TO PYTHIAN APOLLO—
s: Apollo captures the Cretans by leaping onto their ship in the form of a dolphin and directing its course to Crisa. He tells them that they will not return to Cnossos but will serve in his honored temple.

l: the Cretan foundation of Apollo’s sanctuary, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, TO PYTHIAN APOLLO—
s: The Cretans found their service at Apollo’s sanctuary by hauling up their ship, making an altar, offering white meal, and following Apollo to Pytho. They become responsible for guarding the temple and receiving the people who gather there.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, IV. TO HERMES
s: Hermes, son of Zeus and Maia, is born on Cyllene and immediately shows his cunning by inventing the lyre and stealing fifty of Apollo's cattle from Pieria. He disguises the cattle's tracks, drives them to the Alpheus, sacrifices two of them, and returns unseen to his cradle. Apollo discovers the theft, follows the reversed tracks to Hermes, and quarrels with him over the cattle. Hermes and Apollo are then brought before Zeus and the immortals assembled on Olympus for judgment.

l: Hermes, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, IV. TO HERMES
s: Hermes is born to Zeus and Maia on Cyllene. On the day of his birth he invents the lyre, steals fifty of Apollo's cattle, drives them to the Alpheus, sacrifices two of them, and returns unseen to his cradle. He denies the theft to Apollo with elaborate cunning, but is eventually brought with Apollo before Zeus and the immortals on Olympus.

l: Maia, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, IV. TO HERMES
s: Maia is a rich-tressed nymph and a shy goddess who lives in a deep, shady cave on Cyllene. Zeus visits her there, and she gives birth to Hermes on the fourth day of the month. She rebukes Hermes when he returns at night, warning that Apollo may punish him for his actions.

l: Zeus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, IV. TO HERMES
s: Zeus secretly lies with Maia in her cave while Hera sleeps, and Hermes is born from their union. Hermes invokes Zeus as his father while defending himself against Apollo. Zeus is the judge before whom Hermes and Apollo are brought.

l: Apollo, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, IV. TO HERMES
s: Apollo owns the cattle that Hermes steals from Pieria. He follows their strange reversed tracks, questions an old man at Onchestus, discovers Hermes in Maia's cave, and accuses him of the theft. Apollo carries Hermes away, quarrels with him, and brings him to Olympus before Zeus and the immortals.

l: gods, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, IV. TO HERMES
s: The blessed gods are the deathless company among whom Hermes is expected to seek honor and offerings. Apollo searches for his stolen cattle among their divine herds. They gather on Olympus for the judgment of Hermes and Apollo.

l: Cyllene, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, IV. TO HERMES
s: Cyllene is identified as Hermes's domain and as the forest-clad mountain containing Maia's deep-shadowed cave. Hermes is born there and returns there after stealing Apollo's cattle.

l: Pieria, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, IV. TO HERMES
s: Pieria is the place where Apollo's divine cattle are kept and graze in pleasant meadows. Hermes goes there at night, cuts fifty cattle from the herd, and drives them away.

l: Alpheus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, IV. TO HERMES
s: Alpheus is the river to which Hermes drives Apollo's cattle before dawn. Hermes throws his sandals into its deep-eddying water and quenches the fire's embers there.

l: Olympus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, IV. TO HERMES
s: Olympus is the place where Hermes and Apollo arrive after their dispute. Its snowy heights host the assembly of the immortals and the scales of judgment set before Zeus.

l: tortoise, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, IV. TO HERMES
s: Hermes finds a tortoise feeding near Maia's dwelling and treats it as an omen of good luck. He carries it inside, removes its limbs and marrow, and transforms its shell into the body of the first lyre.

l: Apollo’s lyre, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, IV. TO HERMES
s: Hermes makes the lyre from the tortoise's shell, reeds, ox hide, horns, a cross-piece, and seven sheep-gut strings. He tests it, finds that it sounds marvelously, and sings about Zeus, Maia, and his own birth. He keeps it beside him when he returns to his cradle.

l: Apollo's cattle, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, IV. TO HERMES
s: Apollo's cattle are kept in Pieria and include fifty loud-lowing kine stolen by Hermes. Hermes reverses their hoofprints, leads them by a winding route to the Alpheus, and hides the evidence of the theft. He drives them into a byre, feeds them, and sacrifices two cows.

l: the theft of Apollo's cattle, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, IV. TO HERMES
s: Hermes steals Apollo's cattle at night on the day of his birth. He disguises their tracks with reversed hoofprints and woven brushwood sandals, sacrifices two of the cattle, burns the hoofs and heads, and hides the remaining meat. Apollo investigates the missing herd, follows the tracks, and confronts Hermes.

l: Hermes's invention of the lyre, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, IV. TO HERMES
s: Hermes invents the lyre after finding a tortoise outside Maia's cave. He hollows out the shell, fixes reeds across it, stretches ox hide over it, adds horns and seven strings, and makes it sound through his playing.

l: the quarrel between Hermes and Apollo, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, IV. TO HERMES
s: The quarrel begins when Apollo accuses Hermes of stealing his cattle. Hermes denies seeing or taking them, claiming that he is only a newborn concerned with sleep, milk, and swaddling clothes. Apollo calls him a rogue and robber, and the two continue disputing until they are brought before Zeus and the immortals.

l: the assembly on Olympus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, IV. TO HERMES
s: The assembly on Olympus gathers after golden-throned Dawn. Hermes and Apollo are brought before the immortals, and the scales of judgment are set for them before Zeus.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 327-329) Then Hermes and Apollo of the Silver Bow stood at the
s: Hermes is brought before Zeus and Apollo over the theft of Apollo’s cattle, but he cunningly denies the charge. Hermes reveals the lyre, and Apollo, delighted by its music, exchanges his whip and cattle-keeping for it. Apollo and Hermes then become friends, and Apollo gives Hermes a golden staff, limited access to divination, and authority over various animals and omens. Zeus confirms Hermes’ new honors and appoints him messenger to Hades.

l: Hermes, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 327-329) Then Hermes and Apollo of the Silver Bow stood at the
s: Hermes is accused by Apollo of stealing and concealing the cattle, but he artfully denies the theft before Zeus. He reveals and gives the lyre to Apollo, receives the office of cattle-keeping, and is granted authority over omens, various animals, and as messenger to Hades.

l: Apollo, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 327-329) Then Hermes and Apollo of the Silver Bow stood at the
s: Apollo brings Hermes and the cattle theft before Zeus and describes how Hermes drove the cattle toward Pylos and concealed his tracks. He is delighted by the lyre, exchanges his whip for it, becomes Hermes’ friend, and gives Hermes a golden staff and certain prophetic privileges.

l: Zeus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 327-329) Then Hermes and Apollo of the Silver Bow stood at the
s: Zeus hears Apollo’s accusation and Hermes’ denial, laughs at Hermes’ cunning, and orders them to search for the cattle together. He is pleased when they reconcile, confirms Apollo’s promises, and commands that Hermes receive authority over omens, animals, and service as messenger to Hades.

l: the gods of Olympus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 327-329) Then Hermes and Apollo of the Silver Bow stood at the
s: The deathless gods are invoked as the community whose honors and privileges are being negotiated. Apollo promises that Hermes and his mother will gain renown among them, while Hermes is made an omen and trusted messenger among them.

l: the three prophetic sisters, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 327-329) Then Hermes and Apollo of the Silver Bow stood at the
s: The three prophetic sisters are winged virgins who dwell under a ridge of Parnassus and teach divination apart from Apollo. They speak truth when inspired by honey, but speak falsely when deprived of the gods’ sweet food; Apollo gives Hermes access to their instruction.

l: Pylos, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 327-329) Then Hermes and Apollo of the Silver Bow stood at the
s: Pylos is the destination toward which Hermes drives Apollo’s cattle. Hermes and Apollo later return there, reach the ford of Alpheus, and find the cattle in a high-roofed byre.

l: Apollo's cattle, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 327-329) Then Hermes and Apollo of the Silver Bow stood at the
s: The cattle are stolen from Apollo’s meadow, driven toward Pylos, and hidden by Hermes. Apollo and Hermes recover them, and Hermes agrees to graze them so that they will reproduce abundantly.

l: the lyre, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 327-329) Then Hermes and Apollo of the Silver Bow stood at the
s: The lyre produces marvelous music when Hermes plays it and sings while accompanying himself. Apollo is filled with wonder and longing for it, so Hermes gives it to him in exchange for Apollo’s whip and the office of cattle-keeping.

l: Hermes' golden staff, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 327-329) Then Hermes and Apollo of the Silver Bow stood at the
s: Apollo promises Hermes a splendid golden staff with three branches. It is to bring riches and wealth, protect Hermes, and help accomplish every task involving good words or deeds.

l: divination, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 327-329) Then Hermes and Apollo of the Silver Bow stood at the
s: Apollo refuses to teach Hermes the counsel of Zeus, declaring that only Zeus knows it. He nevertheless gives Hermes instruction through the three prophetic sisters and permits him to teach mortals their method when fortune favors them.

l: the theft of Apollo's cattle, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 327-329) Then Hermes and Apollo of the Silver Bow stood at the
s: Apollo accuses Hermes of stealing his cattle and describes the strange tracks leading toward Pylos and Hermes’ concealment of the herd. Hermes denies the theft, but the recovered cattle and the evidence at the cave lead to a settlement between the two gods.

l: the exchange of the lyre and cattle-keeping, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 327-329) Then Hermes and Apollo of the Silver Bow stood at the
s: Hermes gives the lyre to Apollo after Apollo praises its music. Apollo gives Hermes his shining whip and appoints him keeper of the cattle, while Hermes agrees to graze the herd.

l: the oath of friendship, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, (ll. 327-329) Then Hermes and Apollo of the Silver Bow stood at the
s: Hermes promises never to steal anything belonging to Apollo or approach his strong house. Apollo swears to be Hermes’ fellow and friend, to love no other among the immortals, gods, or men sprung from Zeus better than Hermes, and to honor him with gifts and privileges.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, V. TO APHRODITE
s: Aphrodite, who subdues gods, mortals, birds, and beasts through desire, is unable to bend Athene, Artemis, and Hestia. Zeus causes Aphrodite to desire Anchises, a mortal herdsman on Mount Ida, and she disguises herself as a mortal woman before sleeping with him. She reveals her divinity afterward, warns Anchises not to boast of their encounter, and tells him that their son Aeneas will be raised by mountain Nymphs and become a ruler among the Trojans. The hymn contrasts divine immortality with mortal vulnerability, especially through the examples of Ganymedes and Tithonus.

l: Aphrodite, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, V. TO APHRODITE
s: Aphrodite, called golden, laughter-loving, and rich-crowned, stirs sweet passion in gods, mortals, birds, beasts, and all creatures of the sea and land. She cannot bend Athene, Artemis, or Hestia, but she is herself made to desire Anchises and sleeps with him. She later reveals her divinity, foretells the birth of Aeneas, and warns Anchises not to say that he lay with her.

l: gods, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, V. TO APHRODITE
s: The gods are generally subject to Aphrodite’s power, although Athene, Artemis, and Hestia resist her. They are deathless, possess heavenly food and ambrosia, and fear or honor the consequences of divine actions. The gods also include Zeus, who arranges Aphrodite’s encounter with Anchises, and Hermes, who carries messages and brings Aphrodite to Ida.

l: Zeus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, V. TO APHRODITE
s: Zeus is the greatest of the gods and holds the highest majesty, yet Aphrodite can lead his heart astray and mate him with mortal women. He causes Aphrodite to desire Anchises so that she will not mock the gods for mating with mortals. He gives Hestia honor instead of marriage, grants Tros horses in recompense for Ganymedes, makes Tithonus deathless without removing old age, and threatens to strike Anchises with a thunderbolt if he boasts of Aphrodite.

l: Anchises, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, V. TO APHRODITE
s: Anchises is a handsome herdsman tending cattle on Mount Ida and is described as resembling the immortal gods. He welcomes Aphrodite while believing her to be mortal, sleeps with her, and then becomes afraid when he sees her divine form. Aphrodite tells him that he will father Aeneas, but warns him to conceal their union.

l: Hermes, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, V. TO APHRODITE
s: Hermes, called the Slayer of Argus and the immortal Guide, carries Aphrodite away from a gathering of nymphs and marriageable maidens. He tells her that she is to become the wedded wife of Anchises and later returns to the families of the deathless gods. At Zeus’s command, he tells Tros what happened to Ganymedes.

l: Aeneas, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, V. TO APHRODITE
s: Aeneas is the son whom Aphrodite bears after sleeping with Anchises. He is to become a ruler among the Trojans, with descendants continuing after him, and his name is connected with the grief Aphrodite felt when she lay with a mortal. Mountain Nymphs will raise him until he reaches lovely boyhood, after which he is to be brought to Anchises and then taken to windy Ilion.

l: mountain Nymphs, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, V. TO APHRODITE
s: The mountain Nymphs who inhabit Mount Ida are to bring up and rear Aeneas. They are described as neither mortal nor immortal, living for a long time, eating heavenly food, and dancing among the immortals. Their lives are linked to trees that spring up with them and die when their own fates approach.

l: Cyprus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, V. TO APHRODITE
s: Cyprus is Aphrodite’s sweet-smelling home, where her precinct and fragrant altar are located at Paphos. She goes there before dressing herself in rich clothing and traveling toward Troy and Mount Ida.

l: Ida, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, V. TO APHRODITE
s: Mount Ida is a many-fountained, forested mountain where Anchises tends cattle and where Aphrodite finds him alone. It is described as the mother of wild creatures and as the home of mountain Nymphs, who will raise Aeneas there.

l: Troy, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, V. TO APHRODITE
s: Troy is associated with Anchises and his future son Aeneas. Aphrodite travels toward Troy before going to Mount Ida, and she says that Aeneas will reign among the Trojans and later be brought to windy Ilion.

l: love and sexual desire, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, V. TO APHRODITE
s: Aphrodite spreads love and sexual desire among gods, mortals, birds, beasts, and other creatures. Zeus places desire for Anchises in her heart, and she in turn puts desire in the hearts of the animals accompanying her. Desire leads Anchises to sleep with Aphrodite despite believing that she is mortal.

l: marriage, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, V. TO APHRODITE
s: Marriage is refused by Hestia, who chooses to remain a maiden, while Aphrodite tells Anchises that Hermes has decreed that she will be his wedded wife. Aphrodite asks Anchises to present her to his family and prepare a marriage honorable among mortals and gods, though their union is instead concealed after she reveals her identity.

l: the encounter of Aphrodite and Anchises, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, V. TO APHRODITE
s: Aphrodite goes to Mount Ida in the form of a mortal maiden and meets Anchises while he is alone and playing the lyre. Anchises believes her story that she is mortal, takes her to bed, and sleeps with her. Afterward Aphrodite reveals herself, and Anchises fears that lying with a deathless goddess will leave him weakened and miserable.

l: Aeneas’s birth, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, V. TO APHRODITE
s: Aphrodite says that she has conceived a child by Anchises and that the child will be called Aeneas. After he sees the light of the sun, mountain Nymphs will raise him, and he will become a godlike ruler among the Trojans.

l: old age, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, V. TO APHRODITE
s: Old age is described as a harsh and deadly condition that eventually overtakes every mortal man and is dreaded even by the gods. Tithonus receives immortality but not freedom from aging, so he becomes unable to move or lift his limbs and is shut in a room. Aphrodite says that she would not want Anchises to live forever in such a state.

l: divine and mortal nature, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, V. TO APHRODITE
s: The unit contrasts deathless gods with mortal men, who are subject to old age and death. Aphrodite disguises herself as mortal but remains divine, while Anchises is mortal despite resembling the gods in beauty and stature. Their union produces Aeneas, whose divine and mortal ancestry makes him especially godlike among mortal men.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, VI. TO APHRODITE
s: The text praises Aphrodite, whose dominion is the walled cities of sea-set Cyprus. The western wind carries her over the sea in soft foam, where the Hours welcome and dress her in heavenly garments and golden ornaments. The gods welcome Aphrodite and pray to lead her home as a wife because of her beauty. The speaker asks Aphrodite to grant victory in a contest and to order the song.

l: Aphrodite, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, VI. TO APHRODITE
s: Aphrodite is described as stately, gold-crowned, beautiful, and violet-crowned. The western wind carries her over the sea to Cyprus, where the Hours clothe and adorn her; the gods welcome her and pray to take her as a wedded wife. The speaker asks her to grant victory in a contest and to order the song.

l: Cyprus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, VI. TO APHRODITE
s: Cyprus is the place where Aphrodite arrives after being wafted over the sea in soft foam. Aphrodite's dominion is the walled cities of sea-set Cyprus.

l: Horae, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, VI. TO APHRODITE
s: The gold-filleted Hours welcome Aphrodite joyously in Cyprus. They clothe her with heavenly garments, crown her with gold, hang ornaments in her ears, and adorn her with golden necklaces and jewels. They wear these jewels themselves when they go to their father's house to join the lovely dances of the gods.

l: gods, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, VI. TO APHRODITE
s: The gods receive Aphrodite after the Hours have fully decked her and welcome her when they see her. Each god prays that he might lead her home to be his wedded wife because they are amazed at her beauty.

l: song, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, VI. TO APHRODITE
s: The speaker sings of Aphrodite and asks her to order the song. The speaker also says that another song will be remembered.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, VII. TO DIONYSUS
s: Dionysus, son of Semele, is captured by Tyrsenian pirates while appearing as a young man on a shore. When the pirates try to bind him and sail away, vines, ivy, wine, a lion, and a bear appear aboard the ship. The pirates leap into the sea and are changed into dolphins, while Dionysus spares the helmsman and reveals his identity.

l: Dionysus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, VII. TO DIONYSUS
s: Dionysus appears on a headland by the sea as a young man. After the pirates capture him, he causes miraculous signs aboard the ship, changes into a lion, punishes the pirates, spares the helmsman, and identifies himself as the son of Semele and Zeus.

l: Tyrsenian pirates, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, VII. TO DIONYSUS
s: The Tyrsenian pirates seize Dionysus and carry him aboard their ship, intending to force him to reveal his connections and wealth. When they witness his wonders, they flee into the sea and are changed into dolphins.

l: the helmsman, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, VII. TO DIONYSUS
s: The helmsman recognizes that the captive may be a god and urges the crew to release him. Dionysus has mercy on him, holds him back from fleeing, makes him happy, and tells him who he is.

l: the master, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, VII. TO DIONYSUS
s: The master rejects the helmsman's warning and orders the crew to continue sailing with Dionysus captive. When Dionysus appears as a lion, the lion springs upon the master and seizes him.

l: the ship, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, VII. TO DIONYSUS
s: The ship carries Dionysus and the pirates across the sea. Wine flows through it, a vine spreads along its sail, ivy grows around its mast, and its thole-pins become covered with garlands before the crew abandons it.

l: the lion, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, VII. TO DIONYSUS
s: Dionysus changes into a dreadful lion aboard the ship. It roars loudly, glares from the forepeak, and springs upon the master.

l: dolphins, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, VII. TO DIONYSUS
s: The dolphins are the transformed pirates who leap overboard into the bright sea while escaping Dionysus's punishment.

l: the transformation of the pirates into dolphins, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, VII. TO DIONYSUS
s: When the pirates leap overboard to escape the lion and a miserable fate, they are changed into dolphins.

l: the pirates' capture of Dionysus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, VII. TO DIONYSUS
s: The pirates capture Dionysus after finding him on a shore and put him aboard their ship. They try to bind him, but the bonds fall away from his hands and feet.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, VIII. TO ARES
s: The hymn addresses Ares as a powerful, bronze-armored warrior, defender of Olympus, and father of warlike Victory. It asks him to help the speaker gain courage and strength while driving away cowardice and deceitful impulses. The speaker also asks Ares to restrain the fury that leads toward bloodshed and instead grant the boldness to follow the harmless laws of peace.

l: Ares, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, VIII. TO ARES
s: Ares is praised as strong, chariot-riding, golden-helmed, bronze-harnessed, and skilled with the spear. He is described as the Saviour of cities, defender of Olympus, father of warlike Victory, ally of Themis, and leader of righteous men. The speaker asks him for courage and strength, and asks him to restrain the fury that provokes blood-curdling strife.

l: war, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, VIII. TO ARES
s: War is associated with Ares's strength, spear-bearing power, and warlike Victory. The speaker asks for strength of war to drive away cowardice but also asks that violent strife and bloodshed be restrained.

l: Eirene, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, VIII. TO ARES
s: Peace is characterized by harmless laws that the speaker wishes to follow. The speaker asks Ares to grant the boldness to abide within those laws while avoiding strife, hatred, and violent fiends of death.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, IX. TO ARTEMIS
s: The unit is a song to Artemis, the virgin goddess who delights in arrows and was fostered with Apollo. She waters her horses from the Meles and drives her all-golden chariot through Smyrna to vine-clad Claros. At Claros, Apollo waits for her, and the singer begins with Artemis before turning to another song.

l: Artemis, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, IX. TO ARTEMIS
s: Artemis is the virgin sister of the Far-shooter who delights in arrows and was fostered with Apollo. She waters her horses from the Meles and drives her all-golden chariot through Smyrna to vine-clad Claros, where Apollo waits for her.

l: Apollo, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, IX. TO ARTEMIS
s: Apollo is the Far-shooter and the god of the silver bow. He was Artemis’s foster companion and sits waiting for her at vine-clad Claros.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, X. TO APHRODITE
