s: The unit concerns Aphrodite, called Cytherea, a goddess associated with Cyprus and Salamis. She gives kindly gifts to men, and smiles and brightness appear on her lovely face. The speaker greets her and asks her to grant a cheerful song, promising to remember her and another song.

l: Aphrodite, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, X. TO APHRODITE
s: Aphrodite is identified as Cytherea, born in Cyprus, and as the goddess and queen of well-built Salamis and sea-girt Cyprus. She gives kindly gifts to men, with smiles on her lovely face and lovely brightness playing over it; the speaker greets her and asks her to grant a cheerful song.

l: Cyprus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, X. TO APHRODITE
s: Cyprus is described as the birthplace of Cytherea and as sea-girt. Aphrodite is called its queen.

l: song, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, X. TO APHRODITE
s: The speaker sings of Cytherea and asks her to grant a cheerful song. The speaker also says that another song will be remembered.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XI. TO ATHENA
s: The unit is a hymn to Pallas Athene, guardian of the city. It describes her as dread and as loving, with Ares, deeds of war, the sack of cities, shouting, and battle. Athene saves the people as they go out to war and return. The speaker greets her and asks for good fortune and happiness.

l: Pallas Athene, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XI. TO ATHENA
s: Pallas Athene is the guardian of the city. She is dread, loves deeds of war with Ares, and saves the people as they go out to war and come back. She is hailed and asked to give good fortune with happiness.

l: Ares, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XI. TO ATHENA
s: Ares loves deeds of war, the sack of cities, shouting, and battle with Pallas Athene.

l: people, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XI. TO ATHENA
s: The people go out to war and come back. Pallas Athene saves them.

l: war, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XI. TO ATHENA
s: War is associated with deeds of war, the sack of cities, shouting, and battle. The people go out to war and return from it.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XII. TO HERA
s: The unit sings of Hera, whom Rhea bore. Hera is the golden-throned queen of the immortals and is described as surpassing all in beauty. She is the sister and wife of Zeus. The blessed throughout high Olympus reverence and honour Hera as they do Zeus, who delights in thunder.

l: Hera, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XII. TO HERA
s: Hera is the golden-throned queen of the immortals and is described as surpassing all in beauty. Rhea bore her, and she is the sister and wife of Zeus. The blessed throughout high Olympus reverence and honour her.

l: Zeus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XII. TO HERA
s: Zeus is loud-thundering and delights in thunder. He is Hera’s brother and husband, and the blessed throughout high Olympus reverence and honour him.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XIII. TO DEMETER
s: The unit begins a song about rich-haired Demeter and her daughter, lovely Persephone. Demeter is described as an awful goddess. The speaker asks the goddess to keep the city safe and govern the song.

l: Demeter, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XIII. TO DEMETER
s: Demeter is described as rich-haired and an awful goddess. The speaker sings of her and asks her to keep the city safe and govern the song.

l: Persephone, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XIII. TO DEMETER
s: Persephone is identified as Demeter’s lovely daughter. The speaker begins to sing of her.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XIV. TO THE MOTHER OF THE GODS
s: The speaker asks the clear-voiced Muse, daughter of mighty Zeus, to sing about the Mother of all gods and men. The Mother of the Gods is pleased by rattles, timbrels, flutes, wolves, lions, echoing hills, and wooded coombes. The speaker offers a song of greeting to the Mother of the Gods and to all goddesses.

l: Mother of the Gods, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XIV. TO THE MOTHER OF THE GODS
s: The Mother of the Gods is described as the mother of all gods and men. She is well-pleased with the sounds of rattles, timbrels, flutes, wolves, bright-eyed lions, echoing hills, and wooded coombes. The speaker greets her in song.

l: Muse, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XIV. TO THE MOTHER OF THE GODS
s: The Muse, daughter of mighty Zeus, is asked to sing about the Mother of the Gods. She is described as clear-voiced.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XV. TO HERACLES THE LION-HEARTED
s: The hymn praises Heracles, son of Zeus and Alcmena, as the mightiest of men on earth. At Eurystheus's bidding, Heracles wandered over land and sea, performing many violent deeds and enduring many hardships. He now lives happily in snowy Olympus, where he is married to Hebe. The speaker asks Heracles to grant success and prosperity.

l: Heracles, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XV. TO HERACLES THE LION-HEARTED
s: Heracles is the son of Zeus and Alcmena and is called the mightiest of men on earth. He performed many deeds of violence and endured many hardships while wandering over land and sea at Eurystheus's bidding. He now lives happily in Olympus and is married to Hebe.

l: Zeus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, XV. TO HERACLES THE LION-HEARTED
s: Zeus is Heracles's father. He lay with Alcmena before Heracles was born.
